description: Signed an injury settlement release for your child? Legal options do exist. Settlement releases are governed by contract law and may be set aside.
shortAnswer: If you signed an injury settlement release and later discover that your child's injuries are worse, you need to know that legal options do exist. A release is a contract: an attorney may argue that no enforceable contract came into being, or that there are grounds for undoing (rescinding) the agreement.

faq.q: What makes a child injury settlement release an enforceable contract in Georgia?
faq.a: The Courts will enforce a settlement agreement if it can be shown there was a) an offer, b) an acceptance and c) a “meeting of the minds.” Deciding whether a “meeting of the minds” existed at the time of the signing of a release is a fact-specific inquiry that defies generalization.

faq.q: What are grounds for rescinding a settlement release I signed for my child?
faq.a: Possible grounds include overreaching by the insurance company in the way they obtained the release from you, misunderstanding by the parent as to the nature and effect of the release, and mistake of fact as to extent of injury. Mistake of fact is the most difficult kind of grounds to prove.

faq.q: Is a Georgia settlement void if the insurer gave no written notice under O.C.G.A. 33-7-12?
faq.a: O.C.G.A. Section 33-7-12(a) states that a purported settlement is null and void if the third party is not provided with a written notice informing the third party of the lack of consent of the insured. This written notice must be given before the settlement occurs or the settlement is of no effect.

faq.q: Is my child's settlement binding if it was over $15,000 and never approved by a court?
faq.a: If you received more than $15,000.00 from the insurance company and the settlement was not submitted for approval to a court, no legally binding settlement has occurred. You have very good odds of getting the release set aside as unenforceable.
